concept_edges.logic: An array variable stores the memory address of the array, not its elements.
A data structure organizes many values of a data type; the array holds a sequence of values of one type.
Java has eight primitive data types (boolean, char, byte, short, int, long, float, double); each, like any data type, is a set of values and a set of operations on those values.
A variable of a primitive type stores the value itself in its own memory.
System.out.println(s); is itself a statement, so its line of output appears at its own place in the sequence.
When one operand of + is a String, Java converts the other operand to a String before concatenating.
println("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes and then ends the line.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: arithmetic + binds tighter than string-concatenation +
misconceptions.correct_rule: Both uses of + have the same precedence and are evaluated left to right, so "s" + a + b joins a and then b as text; only "s" + (a + b) adds them first.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a(i) accesses element i of an array.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Array elements are accessed with square brackets, a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The number of brackets in an array type or initializer is the array's length.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Brackets give the number of dimensions; the length is set at creation.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array can hold elements of any type.
misconceptions.correct_rule: All elements of an array have the declared element type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a == b is true when a and b hold the same values.
misconceptions.correct_rule: == compares whether the two arrays are the same array, not whether their values are equal.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The first element of a is a[1].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: initializer values go in [] instead of {}
misconceptions.correct_rule: Starting values go in braces, like int[] a = {v0, v1};.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an ArrayList is an array (borderline; beyond Chapter 1 CS1)
misconceptions.correct_rule: An array has a fixed length and uses [] and .length; an ArrayList can grow and uses get, set and size().

misconceptions.wrong_belief: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The slots are 0 to n - 1.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Using an array means every cell must be scanned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Arrays allow random access: a[i] reaches one element directly, and a loop visits only the elements the task needs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: assigning a reference copies the object
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The declaration only names the array; until new (or an initializer) creates it, using a[i] gives a 'variable might not have been initialized' compile-time error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i.
misconceptions.correct_rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is used.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: X[i] names the whole array, not one element.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The array is a; a[i] is the single element at index i.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: == compares contents (the String == bug)
misconceptions.correct_rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The slots of a new int[n] hold unpredictable values until assigned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: new fills every element with a default: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for String and other non-primitive types.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: () are optional on a no-argument call like println
misconceptions.correct_rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: print and println behave the same (no newline difference)
misconceptions.correct_rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: println(s) prints a newline and then s.
misconceptions.correct_rule: println(s) prints s and then the newline.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes a string literal in single quotes: 'Hello'.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String literals use double quotes; single quotes are for one char.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a statement runs without the ;
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement must end with ;, otherwise javac reports ';' expected.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Statements in a program can run in any order.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: String is a primitive type like int.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Breaks a string literal across two lines of code.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String literals must not span more than one line of a program.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text.
misconceptions.correct_rule: + is evaluated left to right: 2 + 3 + "bc" is "5bc" but "bc" + 2 + 3 is "bc23".

misconceptions.wrong_belief: + with a String turns the whole other side into a string first
misconceptions.correct_rule: The expression (a + b) is evaluated first, and its value is then turned into text and joined to s.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A string literal can be left without its closing quote.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A String literal is enclosed in a pair of double quotes.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference
misconceptions.correct_rule: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java compilers consider all whitespace in program text (outside quotation marks) to be equivalent; layout is for human readers.

level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: a == b is true when a and b hold the same values. Right rule: == compares whether a and b are the same array (same reference), not whether their elements are equal.
wrong rule: Assigning an array reference copies the array. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].

Points to LT: b = a copies the reference, so every later write through b is a write to the shared array. Inconsistent application: after b = a the trace changes b[0] but leaves a[0] unchanged in its table, keeping two copies on some steps and one array on others. (here mixing in: "a == b is true when a and b hold the same values")

Conservation: replacing b = a with an element-copy loop keeps b's initial contents but breaks the link, so later changes to a no longer show in b. Reassigning a = new int[n] after b = a leaves b on the old array.

wrong rule: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed. Right rule: The declaration only names the array variable; until new (or an initializer) creates the array, a[i] gives the compile-time error 'variable a might not have been initialized'.
wrong rule: An array can hold elements of any type. Right rule: Every element of an array has the declared element type: an int[] holds only int values, a String[] only String references.

wrong rule: The number of brackets in an array type is the array's length. Right rule: Each bracket pair adds one dimension (int[] is 1-D, int[][] is 2-D); the length is not part of the type and is fixed only when the array is created.

Points to LT: declare, then create, then initialize, in that order. Inconsistent application: the trace treats a as already created on some lines (reading a[i] straight after 'int[] a;') while requiring new on others. (here mixing in: "int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed")
wrong rule: X[i] names the whole array, not one element. Right rule: The name a (written a[] in the book) denotes the whole array; a[i] denotes the single element at index i.

Conservation: rewriting 'int[] a' as 'int a[]' keeps the meaning. Changing the element type changes which values may be stored and the default values. Deleting the creation step breaks the program at compile time.
wrong rule: Initializer values go in [] instead of {}. Right rule: Starting values go in braces, as in int[] a = {v0, v1};; brackets only mark the type or an index.

Points to LT: an array of length k+1 is created, then v0..vk are stored at indices 0..k in order. Inconsistent application: the trace puts the first value at index 1 for one initializer but at index 0 for another, or counts the length differently. (here mixing in: "initializer values go in [] instead of {}")

wrong rule: The number of brackets in an array type or initializer is the array's length. Right rule: Brackets give the number of dimensions; an initializer's length is the number of values between its braces.

Conservation: adding or removing a value changes the length. Code that uses a.length (e.g. rank.length) adapts, while code with a hard-coded size breaks. Reordering values changes which index holds which value.

wrong rule: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division. Right rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

Points to LT (find each operand's type, then apply that type's operator). Applied unevenly, a student uses the int operator for 7 / 2 in one line (3) but real division in the next (3.5), or treats a String "12" as a number in one + and as text in another. (here mixing in: "Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division")

Widening a variable's type (int to double) usually still compiles but changes which operations run: / keeps fractions and output prints 3.0. Narrowing it (double to int) breaks every assignment of a double value with a compile-time error. Values that fit both types are kept.
wrong rule: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value. Right rule: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.
wrong rule: The first element of a is a[1]. Right rule: Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].
wrong rule: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive. Right rule: The slots are 0 to n - 1.
wrong rule: a(i) accesses element i of an array. Right rule: Array elements are selected with square brackets, a[i]; a(i) would be a call of a method named a.

wrong rule: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]]. Right rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.
wrong rule: X[i] names the whole array, not one element. Right rule: The array is a (a[] in the book); a[i] is the single element at index i.
wrong rule: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i. Right rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is executed.

Points to LT: in a[i], a is evaluated, then i with its current value, then the bounds check, then the element is read or written. Inconsistent application: i is updated on one line, but a later a[i] is traced with the old i. (here mixing in: "i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value")
wrong rule: Using an array means every cell must be scanned. Right rule: Arrays allow random access: a[i] reaches one element directly, and a loop visits only the elements the task needs.

Conservation: changing the index expression (i to i+1 or i-1) shifts which element is touched and can leave the bounds at the ends. Writing a[a[i]] instead of a[i] uses an element value as the index, a different access entirely. Changing what is stored never changes the positions.
wrong rule: String is a primitive type like int. Right rule: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).

Points to LT (each operation is done in its type's fixed size). Applied unevenly, a student truncates and wraps int results on one line but treats another int intermediate as an unbounded real number, e.g. tracing 59 / 60 * 100 as 98. (here mixing in: "String is a primitive type like int")

wrong rule: The slots of a new int[n] hold unpredictable values until assigned. Right rule: new fills every element with a default: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for String and other non-primitive types.

Switching one primitive type for another changes range and precision. int to long removes overflow up to about 9.2e18. int to double keeps fractions but stops being exact for very large integers. Changing a type to boolean breaks every arithmetic use.
wrong rule: A reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference. Right rule: An array variable stores a reference (the memory address) to the array, not the elements.

Applies the model unevenly: treats int x = y as copying a value (correct) but also treats b = a for arrays as copying all the elements. (here mixing in: "a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference")
wrong rule: String is a primitive type like int. Right rule: Java has eight primitive types; String is not one of them, and a String variable holds a reference.
Conservation: changing a primitive copy never affects the original; changing an array through any reference affects every alias.
wrong rule: print and println behave the same. Right rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.
wrong rule: println(s) prints a newline and then s. Right rule: println(s) prints s and then the line terminator.

Applies the println rule (print, then end line) unevenly: puts the newline before the text on one call and after it on another, or forgets that the next output starts on a new line. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.
Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.
wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values the programmer meant. Right rule: The computer executes only the statements written; every needed step and value must be written.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: executes the statements in order on some lines but lets a later statement's effect leak into an earlier one, or skips or repeats a statement on one pass. (here mixing in: "The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command")
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order, so their order makes no difference. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom, in the order written.

wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers treat all whitespace outside quotes as equivalent; statements are separated by ;, not by line breaks.

wrong rule: The program knows what later lines will do and acts on that goal at the current line. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
Swapping two statements that touch the same variable or the output generally changes the result; swapping independent statements, or changing only whitespace between them, keeps it.
wrong rule: + with a String turns the whole other side into a string first. Right rule: The expression (a + b) is evaluated first, and its value is then turned into text and joined to s.
wrong rule: 2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text. Right rule: + is evaluated left to right: 2 + 3 + "bc" is "5bc" but "bc" + 2 + 3 is "bc23".

Points to LT (left to right, and each + adds or concatenates according to its operands at that moment). Applied unevenly, a student keeps adding numbers after a String has appeared, or concatenates before any String appears (1 + 2 + "x" as "12x"). (here mixing in: "+ with a String turns the whole other side into a string first")

wrong rule: arithmetic + binds tighter than string-concatenation +. Right rule: Both uses of + have the same precedence and are evaluated left to right, so "s" + a + b joins a and then b as text; only "s" + (a + b) adds them first.

Parenthesizing numeric parts changes the result ("sum " + (a + b) adds before joining). Moving numbers before or after the first String changes whether they are added. Concatenating into a printf format string removes the separate argument printf needs.
wrong rule: 2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text. Right rule: + is evaluated left to right: 2 + 3 + "bc" is "5bc" but "bc" + 2 + 3 is "bc23".

Points to LT (+ is applied left to right, each + deciding between addition and concatenation from its two operands at that moment). Applied unevenly: once a String has appeared the student goes back to numeric addition for later terms, or concatenates two numbers that come before any String. (here mixing in: "2 + 3 + "bc" and "bc" + 2 + 3 give the same text")
Adding parentheses around the numeric part changes "bc23" into "bc5"; moving a String operand earlier turns every later + into concatenation; the order of operands matters, unlike numeric addition.
